newsitem.title: MEXICO: Stockwatchers see smooth ride for Mexico elections.
newsitem.headline: Stockwatchers see smooth ride for Mexico elections.

text.p: Foreign investors are plowing money into Mexico's stock market on a scale not seen since the 1994 peso crisis, betting that upcoming elections will not spoil bull market sentiment, market watchers say.

Inflows of foreign capital have made for a recent batch of historic gains on the Mexican bourse. The market chalked up its fourth record close in a row on Monday when it gained 15.21 points, or 0.36 percent, to 4,259.84.
So far this month, the market has climbed 7.3 percent.

Although the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) could lose its lower house majority for the first time since 1929, investors are betting the PRI will either keep its majority or at least keep its economic policies from being derailed.
"Political risk has begun to decline," said Jorge Mariscal, chief investment strategist for Latin America at Goldman Sachs in New York.
"There is evidence of a recovery in the domestic sector, although it is in its early stages ... The feeling is investors have to buy before the elections."

"There is a real sense of calmness about the upcoming elections," said Geoffrey Dennis, global emerging markets strategist at HSBC-James Capel in New York. "Investors do not see any cathartic political developments."
Mexico will hold elections on July 6 to renew the entire lower house of Congress, one-quarter of the Senate, the first vote for Mexico City mayor in modern times and several state governors.
An opposition majority in the Congress could "be a partial negative," Dennis added, "due to fear of the unknown."
Wrangling between the executive and legislature over budgetary and economic policy has been virtually absent from modern Mexico.

Nonetheless, Dennis said a likely victory in Mexico City by the main center-left opposition candidate, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, was unlikley to spill over into the Congress and trigger a sudden shift in economic policy.
"A win in Mexico City does not mean Cardenas will run the country per se," he said.

A string of recent opinion polls show a wide margin for the Mexico City mayoral race in favor of Cardenas, from the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), but show the leftist party still trailing both the PRI and the conservative National Action Party in the country as a whole.
Felix Boni, research director at ING-Barings in Mexico, also downplayed "excessive" worry over the vote, saying the immediate economic impact of a Cardenas victory would be limited.
"Tactically, he (Cardenas) wouldn't be able to do anything as Mexico City mayor," he said. "The pressure point will be the outcome in Congress."
Under Mexican electoral rules, even if the PRI does not poll an overall majority for the lower chamber, it could still be awarded a majority of seats with just 42 percent of the vote.
"The market is coming to terms with the elections, where it seems the PRI will not do too well, but that's in the price," said Perry Winfield, head of Latin American research at Paribas.
Ramon Ruiz, sales trader at Latinvest in New York, said he had seen investors buy Mexican stocks in advance of what they saw as a smooth electoral process.
"There seems to be a correlation between proximity and expectations of a calm and fair process. The closer we get, the stabler we get," he said.
"The market has clearly discounted a Cardenas victory (in Mexico City), but is exhibiting faith the PRI will do well, or have a fighting chance, in the lower house," he added.
